name: Arandai, Sebyar dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1985. Some notes on the Arandai language, South Bird's Head, Irian Jaya. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya 13 (XIII): 3-40.
catalog_locator: p. 7, sec. 2.2.4 'Stress' (within sec. 2.0 'Weriagar'; p. 7, right half of the 2-up scan); p. 17, sec. 3.0 'Sebyar' (p. 12 right); p. 19, sec. 4.0 (p. 13 right); p. 4 for informants and the sec. 2.0 heading (p. 6 left).
catalog_quote: 2.2.4 Stress. Stress placement is not predictable and is in fact phonemic as is shown by the minimal pair [ˈařaǰa] 'wave' - [ařˈaǰa] 'salty'. Examples of variation in stress placement are [kˈɑǰo] 'grub', [au̯ˈi] 'heron', [met̪akˈɔ] 'wing', [it̪ˈane] 'sun', [ˈuřaŋge] 'rain'. [p. 17, sec. 3.0 Sebyar:] Phonetically Sebyar is very similar to the Weriagar dialect, but the data collected so far favour a somewhat different phonemic analysis. ... The vowel system seems to be the same as that of Weriagar. [p. 19, sec. 4.0, quoting Anceaux 1958 on Barau:] "Final vowels, not having the accent, tend to get nearly inaudible or even to disappear. The accent consists of a high pitch. A vowel preceding the accent (if there is one) is prolonged. There seems to be no simple rule for the place of the accent in polysyllable words." Judging by the Weriagar data Anceaux was right regarding the absence of tense markers in the verb, the freedom of accent placement, and the behaviour of word-final vowels. But in Weriagar it is the stressed vowel which is lengthened and stress is not always marked by a high pitch.
world_status: statement found in an open source

(2) p.12 r…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free/lexical: its position cannot be predicted from the shape of the word and distinguishes minimal pairs; it may fall on the initial, a medial, or the final syllable. The stressed vowel is lengthened; high pitch is not a consistent correlate (contra Anceaux's description of Barau accent as high pitch with lengthening of the pre-accent vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; Anceaux (quoted p.19) notes for Barau that unaccented final vowels tend to become nearly inaudible or disappear, which Voorhoeve confirms for Weriagar.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based on elicited citation forms and short phrases from one Weriagar speaker (about 6 hours) and one Sebyar speaker (about 3 hours), survey data collected Aug-Sep 1982. The explicit statement is made in the Weriagar section; Sebyar (Dombano proper) is covered only by 'phonetically very similar' plus stress-marked forms showing varying position (ˈnendi, ˈandi, uˈma, maniˈago, manduˈaygo, botˈanomo, dangˈamo).
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve's 'Arandai language' spans two Glottolog languages: Dombano aran1237 [jbj] = his Sebyar dialect (villages Tomu, Arandai, Kecap; his Sebyar data are from a Tomu speaker) and Kemberano kemb1235 [bzp] = his Weriagar and Barau dialects (his Tarof and Kasuweri are now assigned to Kokoda). The explicit stress statement (sec. 2.2.4, p.7) is made for the Weriagar dialect, i.e. strictly Kemberano kemb1235; for Sebyar/Dombano proper the source says only 'Phonetically Sebyar is very similar to the Weriagar dialect' (p.17) and cites Sebyar forms with stress marked in varying positions. The same quote can serve kemb1235 directly. Glottolog itself files Voorhoeve 1985 as the Glottolog's most extensive description grammar sketch for aran1237.
